opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, thanks for having me. So I think the core reason distillation through synthetic data works so well is that it changes *what* the student model gets to learn from. When you pretrain or fine-tune on human-written data, you're learning from text that wasn't produced with your model in mind. It's noisy, it skips steps, it reflects whatever the author happened to know. When a stronger teacher generates the data, you can shape it: you get full reasoning traces, consistent formatting, coverage of exactly the kinds of problems you care about, and you can generate as much of it as you want.

There's also the information you get per example. If you do something like on-policy or logit-level distillation, the student doesn't just see the single "correct" token. It sees the teacher's whole distribution, which tells it which alternatives were plausible and how confident to be. That's a much richer training signal than a one-hot label, and it's a big part of why small models trained this way punch above their weight.

And one thing I've found really interesting in our work is that it doesn't even have to be the biggest, most capable teacher. If you think about it compute-matched, sometimes sampling many more solutions from a smaller, cheaper model and filtering them for correctness gives you better training data than sampling a handful from a big model. You get more coverage and more diversity, and verification takes care of a lot of the quality issues. So it's really about the trade-off between quality, diversity, and cost, not just "use the strongest model."

The last piece is the connection to self-improvement. Once you have a verifier, like unit tests for code or checking final answers in math, synthetic data becomes a loop: generate, filter, train, repeat. That's essentially reinforcement learning with a very simple reward, and it lets models improve beyond the human data they started with. So for me distillation isn't just compression. It's one of the most practical tools we have for moving capability around and building on it.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the simplest way to put it is that synthetic-data distillation is the cheapest way we have of moving capability from a model that has it to a model that doesn't. You take a strong teacher, you sample solutions from it on problems you care about, you filter those solutions for correctness, and you fine-tune a smaller or earlier model on what survives. That's it. There's no gradient flowing from the teacher, no need to match logits, no need to even have the teacher's weights. You just need its outputs.

And the reason that matters is that the bottleneck for most people isn't compute at training time, it's data. Human-written data for reasoning tasks, math, code, multi-step problems, is scarce and expensive, and it's not getting cheaper. But a good model can generate millions of attempts at those problems overnight. So suddenly the limiting factor is whether you can verify what's correct, and for a lot of domains you can. Math has answers. Code has tests. That verification step is doing a lot of the work. It turns an unbounded stream of model outputs into something that looks like a curated dataset.

The thing that surprised me, and this is something we spent a while studying, is that the teacher doesn't actually have to be a bigger model. One of the results I keep coming back to is that if you have a fixed sampling budget, you're often better off generating a lot of samples from a smaller, weaker model than fewer samples from a larger, stronger one. The weaker model covers more of the problem space, you get more diverse solutions, and even though it's wrong more often, the filtering catches most of that. The student ends up learning more. That really changed how I think about it. It's not "big model teaches small model." It's "sampling plus verification is a general-purpose data factory," and the model at the front of that factory can be whatever gives you the best coverage per dollar.

The other reason I like it is that it composes with everything else. You can use it as a warm start before RL so the policy isn't starting from zero on hard problems. You can use it to iterate on the same model, where the model generates, you filter, you train, and you repeat, which is basically expert iteration, and that works surprisingly well. And it's a clean way to transfer capabilities across model generations, so when you train a new base model you're not throwing away everything the previous one learned.

I'd be honest that there are failure modes. If your filter is weak you learn the teacher's mistakes. If you only distill final answers you can lose a lot of the reasoning the teacher actually did. And there's a real question about whether you're just redistributing capability versus creating new capability. But as a practical tool, if someone asked me what single technique has the best ratio of simplicity to impact in the LLM post-training toolbox right now, this would be my answer.

astra-6.text:
I think the key idea is that generating a good answer and learning from a good answer are different problems. A strong model can spend a lot of computation exploring solutions, checking its work, and producing examples. Then a smaller model can learn from those examples and become much cheaper to run.

Synthetic data also gives you control over what you train on. If the student struggles with a particular kind of task, you can generate more examples in that area, rather than hoping those examples show up in a web corpus. That makes distillation a useful way to turn a general capability into something more targeted.

The caveat is that generating more data doesn’t automatically mean generating more useful data. You need diversity, quality checks, and a way to tell whether the student is actually improving. Otherwise, you can just amplify the teacher’s mistakes. But when that loop works, it’s a powerful way to make capabilities more accessible.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the useful framing is that synthetic data lets you turn compute into a learning signal. You can have a stronger model spend a lot of effort solving a problem—generate multiple candidates, check them, refine them—and then train a smaller model on the successful results. You’re paying that cost upfront so the smaller model can produce useful answers much more cheaply at inference time.

It also gives you control over what the model practices. If it struggles with a particular kind of task, you can generate more examples in that area instead of waiting to find the right data on the internet.

The caveat is that generating more text isn’t automatically generating more knowledge. You need diversity and a reliable way to select good outputs. When you can verify the answers, synthetic-data distillation becomes particularly powerful: you can turn a relatively expensive search process into a capability the model learns to use directly.
